ctx.x: All right, now, we're talking to Earl Humphrey. Today is November 30th, 1968. Now, could you tell us about when you were playing with Buddy Petit? What is all you can remember about Buddy Petit?

Well, I suppose it must have been just about 1926. And we had a gig over in Mandeville every other Saturday night. In the hotel. Buddy was stationed over there with another man. And it looks as though he had gotten tired of being over there, kind of lonesome, just working on weekends. So he decided to come home and join us in the Orleans with Lee Collins and Earl Humphrey's band. That was our band. So you mean you had two companies? We only had one until Buddy joined us. So Buddy, he got on the train. We wasn't…

items.title: Earl Humphrey Interview, 1968-11-30
items.q: Interviewer mentions 'Buddy the T' as an example of a band that wasn't recorded; Interviewee does not mention Buddy the T or claim any personal interaction.

ctx.x: Yeah, before then. Because I went off on the road that night. Yeah. I'd gone down to Crowley, Louisiana, playing with the Black Eagle, playing.

Yeah. Another thing it seems to me, there were certain bands, maybe this is true, there were certain bands that maybe had a style more on like today's style. I mean, they just weren't ever recorded. You see, like, take Chris Kelly or Buddy the T, you know, they were recorded. Yeah, they never recorded. And it seems like they were probably had more, more swing, more jazz to them. You know, you'd say some of those bands, like Sam Morgan's band, or more, or, of course, the Piron band, you know, it was just more…

Well, it's like I tell you, see, all, all the bands, now you listen to them around there every night. It's a different than every band come in there. But it's similar on the same style, but no two musicians in town plays exactly alike. Not only in town, that is when you routine it. No two or no place plays exactly alike. But they're similar, you know, you can tell, you can distinct, tell that you, it's similar to the others, you know. But it's not exactly alike. You get used to them, you can stand outside and…

items.title: Earl Humphrey Interview, 1963-03-28
items.q: Father, he's a great father of Buddy Petit.

ctx.x: at, at, uh, Abbeville and Franklin, customized in Franklin. Yeah. Well, anyhow, that's where

we stopped at. But he know he had, he know he had friends there, see. Yeah. I walked over there. And, uh, Baptiste was there. What is Baptiste? He was a gambler, trumpet player. He told, uh, Baptiste said, what you gonna do today? I said, well, Baptiste used to take lessons from him. You know what I mean. Father, he's a great father of Buddy Petit. Mm-hmm. I'll call you home. You dig.

I asked him, say, where you gonna sleep at? Well, I bet he had a rooming house down the street. But he said, I ain't got nowhere to play, I ain't going home. And that's going, what time you got a play? Well, we supposed to start that appetite in that day at one o'clock. It was about nine o'clock then. And, uh, boy went and took him a nap and everything, you know. He had the horn with him, he got that horn. And we gonna meet, uh, Third and Willa, baseball players and all, you know, make a little appetizer and all.
